held.title: Reads after cleanup() now fail with ErrStreamClosed instead of reaching the upstream.
held.body: Before this change, `cleanup()` only stopped the timer, and later `Read` calls still went to the underlying reader. Now `cleanup` sets `stopped`, and `startRead` returns false for every later `Read`, so the caller gets `ErrStreamClosed` (or `ErrStreamIdleTimeout` if the timer fired earlier). A caller that calls `cleanup()` (or a disarm helper built on it) early to turn off idle detection and then keeps reading or draining the body, for example after `finish_reason`, would now lose the rest of the stream. The request asks only to limit the timeout to pending reads; it does not ask to stop reads after cleanup. I couldn't see the call sites, so check that no caller reads after `cleanup()`. If one does, make `stopped` only disarm the timer and let `Read` pass straight through to `r.reader`.

held.title: Each zero-byte Read now restarts the idle deadline, so a stream that keeps returning (0, nil) never times out.
held.body: Before, only reads that returned `n > 0` reset the timer, so an upstream that kept returning `(0, nil)` was still treated as idle. That is what the removed `ZeroBytesDoNotResetTimer` test checked. Now `startRead` sets a fresh deadline and resets the timer on every `Read` call, whatever the previous call returned. A misbehaving upstream or decoder that returns zero bytes with no error in a loop keeps the timer re-armed forever, and the idle timeout never fires. The renamed test only covers one zero-byte read followed by a stall. To fix, keep a 'last progress' time that only reads with `n > 0` update, and base the deadline on it, while still disarming the timer between reads.
